Approximation Theory of Laplacian-Based Neural Operators for Reaction-Diffusion Systems

Takashi Furuya Address: Doshisha University, RIKEN AIP, Japan Email address: tfuruya@mail.doshisha.ac.jp , Ryo Ozawa Address: Tohoku University, Japan Email address: ozawa.ryo.q6@dc.tohoku.ac.jp and Jenn-Nan Wang  Address: Institute of Applied Mathematical Sciences, National Taiwan University, Taipei 106, Taiwan. Email address: jnwang@math.ntu.edu.tw
Abstract.

Neural operators provide a framework for learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling efficient surrogate modeling for complex systems. While universal approximation results are now well understood, quantitative approximation analysis specific to nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems remains limited. In this paper, we study Laplacian-based neural operators applied to the solution mapping from initial conditions to time-dependent solutions of nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. By exploiting the Laplacian spectral representation of the diffusion semigroup, we obtain polynomial complexity bounds on the network depth, width, and spectral rank, demonstrating that Laplacian eigenfunction-based neural operators can exploit the structure of the underlying PDE while avoiding the curse of parametric complexity encountered in generic operator learning. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and illustrate the benefit of Laplacian eigenfunction representations compared with Fourier-based spectral representations.

1. Introduction

Reaction-diffusion equations constitute a fundamental class of partial differential equations (PDEs) that describe the interplay between local reactions and spatial diffusion. They arise naturally in numerous scientific disciplines, including chemical kinetics, biology, ecology, materials science, and neuroscience. Classical examples include the Fisher-KPP equation for population dynamics [9, 17], the Gierer-Meinhardt system for self-organized pattern formation [13], the Gray-Scott model for chemical pattern formation [14, 30], and the FitzHugh-Nagumo system for nerve impulse propagation [10, 29]. Owing to their rich nonlinear dynamics, reaction-diffusion systems exhibit a wide variety of phenomena, including traveling waves, Turing patterns, and spatiotemporal oscillations. Consequently, they serve as important mathematical models in both applied sciences and numerical analysis.

Classical numerical methods, such as finite difference, finite element, and spectral methods, provide accurate approximations of reaction-diffusion equations. However, these approaches often become computationally expensive when repeated simulations are required for varying initial conditions, model parameters, or forcing terms. Such many-query settings frequently arise in uncertainty quantification, inverse problems, optimization, and real-time prediction. These challenges have motivated the development of learning-based surrogate models that approximate the underlying solution operators rather than individual solutions.

Among recent advances in scientific machine learning, neural operators have emerged as a powerful framework for learning mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces. Unlike conventional neural networks, which approximate finite-dimensional input-output relationships, neural operators are designed to learn operators that map input functions directly to output functions while remaining applicable across different discretizations. Representative neural operator architectures include the Graph Neural Operator [25], the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) [24], the Wavelet Neural Operator [33, 15], the Spherical Fourier Neural Operator [1], the Laplace Neural Operator [4], and, more recently, continuum transformer neural operators [2]. These architectures have demonstrated remarkable empirical success across a broad range of PDEs while offering mesh-independent representations, efficient inference after training, and strong generalization across families of input functions.

The expressive power of neural operators is supported by a growing body of theoretical work. Universal approximation theorems for classical neural networks were first established by Cybenko [7] and later extended to operators between function spaces by Chen and Chen [6]. Building on these foundational results, universal approximation theorems have been proved for several neural operator architectures, including DeepONets [26, 21], Fourier Neural Operators [19], Analytic Neural Operators [20], and continuum transformer neural operators [2]. Moreover, neural operators have been shown to approximate both the forward and inverse Calderón maps arising in inverse conductivity problems [3], further demonstrating their ability to learn nonlinear solution operators.

Besides expressivity, the efficiency of neural operators is an equally important theoretical consideration. General neural operators satisfying only mild regularity assumptions may suffer from the curse of parametric complexity, whereby the number of trainable parameters grows exponentially with the desired approximation accuracy [22]. Fortunately, this phenomenon can often be avoided for structured solution operators arising from well-posed PDEs. Quantitative approximation results have been established for Fourier Neural Operators applied to Darcy flow and the Navier-Stokes equations [19], PCA-Net [23], Hamilton-Jacobi neural operators [22], nonlinear parabolic equations [11], scattering operators [12], and DeepONets for elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic PDEs [5, 21, 27, 8]. Collectively, these results demonstrate that neural operators can efficiently approximate many PDE solution operators while maintaining favorable approximation complexity.

1.1. Related work

The results above suggest a broader principle: quantitative operator approximation can be substantially improved by exploiting the structure of the underlying PDE rather than treating its solution operator as a generic infinite-dimensional map. This motivates neural operator architectures whose nonlocal components are adapted to the differential operator governing the PDE.

A prominent example is the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) [24], whose nonlocal layers are parameterized in the Fourier domain. Fourier representations are particularly natural for PDEs on periodic or rectangular domains and enable efficient implementations through the FFT. However, on a general bounded domain with prescribed boundary conditions, the Fourier basis need not reflect the geometry of the domain or the boundary conditions of the underlying PDE.

For diffusion-dominated PDEs, a natural alternative is to exploit the spectral structure of the Laplacian itself. The eigenfunctions of the Laplacian are closely tied to the diffusion dynamics and depend on both the geometry of the domain and the prescribed boundary conditions. They therefore provide a PDE-adapted basis, rather than a generic representation of spatial functions. This motivates Laplacian-based neural operators, whose nonlocal layers are constructed using truncated Laplacian eigenfunction expansions.

Laplacian eigenfunctions have recently been incorporated into operator-learning architectures; see, for example, [16, 4]. These approaches demonstrate the potential benefit of geometry- and boundary-aware spectral representations. Our focus is complementary: rather than only using Laplacian eigenfunctions as an architectural choice, we study quantitatively why such a representation is well suited to nonlinear parabolic PDE systems. In particular, the same Laplacian spectrum simultaneously determines the linear diffusion semigroup and the spectral truncation appearing in the neural operator. This correspondence allows the approximation complexity of the architecture to be related directly to spectral properties of the underlying PDE.

Our work is also closely related to the quantitative approximation theory of [11] for scalar nonlinear parabolic equations. That work introduced a PDE-specific approximation strategy based on the mild formulation and Picard iteration, but treated the approximation of the underlying integral operator through an abstract finite-rank approximation assumption. The present work instead considers nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems and makes the spectral approximation explicit by exploiting the Laplacian semigroup.

The distinction from existing Laplacian-based operator-learning results is also worth emphasizing. For example, the approach of [16] is based on a DeepONet-type architecture, whereas we analyze a neural operator whose nonlocal layers reproduce truncated Laplacian semigroup and Duhamel propagators. More importantly, our objective is a quantitative approximation theory that simultaneously controls the network depth, the number of neurons, and the spectral rank required for approximating the full time-dependent solution operator of a nonlinear reaction-diffusion system.

1.2. Contributions

Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    Quantitative approximation theory for nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. We develop a quantitative approximation theory for neural operators applied to nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. Rather than treating the solution map as a generic operator, our analysis starts from its mild formulation and constructs the neural operator by approximating the associated Picard iteration. This provides explicit approximation guarantees for the solution operator mapping initial conditions to full time-dependent trajectories, with network complexity that grows polynomially with respect to the target accuracy.

  • •

    Laplacian-based neural operators that exploit PDE structure. We construct the nonlocal layers from Laplacian eigenfunctions associated with the boundary conditions of the PDE. The resulting architecture is directly motivated by the spectral representation of the diffusion semigroup: the basis functions encode the domain geometry and boundary conditions, while the corresponding exponential multipliers encode the diffusion dynamics. Thus, the architecture incorporates the structure of the underlying PDE at the level of its nonlocal operator. Numerical experiments support the theoretical motivation and demonstrate the effectiveness of the Laplacian-based representation compared with standard Fourier-based representations.

U(L+1)​(x,t):=W(L)​U(L)​(x,t)+(K(L)​U(L))​(x,t)+b(L).\displaystyle U^{(L+1)}(x,t):=W^{(L)}U^{(L)}(x,t)+(K^{(L)}U^{(L)})(x,t)+b^{(L)}.

Here, σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} denotes a nonlinear activation function applied element-wise. For each hidden layer ℓ\ell, W(ℓ)∈ℝrℓ+1×rℓW^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell+1}\times r_{\ell}} is a weight matrix and b(ℓ)∈ℝrℓ+1b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell+1}} is a bias vector. The operator

K(ℓ):L∞​([0,T],L∞​(Ω,ℝrℓ))→L∞​([0,T],L∞​(Ω,ℝrℓ+1))K^{(\ell)}:L^{\infty}([0,T];L^{\infty}(\Omega,{\mathbb{R}}^{r_{\ell}}))\to L^{\infty}([0,T];L^{\infty}(\Omega,{\mathbb{R}}^{r_{\ell+1}}))

is a nonlocal operator defined by

(K(ℓ)​u~)​(x,t):=∑j≤NC(ℓ,1)​(∫0t∫ΩEj​(t−s)​C(ℓ,2)​u~​(y,s)​ϕj​(y)​𝑑y​𝑑s)​ϕj​(x),\displaystyle(K^{(\ell)}\tilde{u})(x,t):=\sum_{j\leq N}C^{(\ell,1)}\left(\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\Omega}E_{j}(t-s)C^{(\ell,2)}\tilde{u}(y,s)\phi_{j}(y)dyds\right)\phi_{j}(x),

where C(ℓ,1)∈ℝrℓ+1×mC^{(\ell,1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell+1}\times m} and C(ℓ,2)∈ℝm×rℓC^{(\ell,2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r_{\ell}} are trainable matrices. By construction, rL+1=mr_{L+1}=m, so that the output dimension matches the mm-component state variable uu.

The collection of learnable parameters is given by

{W(ℓ),b(ℓ),C(0),C(ℓ,1),C(ℓ,2)}ℓ=1L.\{W^{(\ell)},\,b^{(\ell)},\,C^{(0)},\,C^{(\ell,1)},\,C^{(\ell,2)}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}.

We denote by 𝒩​𝒪σL,H,N\mathcal{NO}^{L,H,N}_{\sigma} the class of neural operators defined above, characterized by the depth LL, the total number of neurons H=∑ℓ=1LrℓH=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}r_{\ell}, the spectral rank NN, and the activation function σ\sigma.

This neural operator exploits the Laplacian eigenfunction basis through the nonlocal operators K(ℓ)K^{(\ell)}. In contrast to standard FNOs, which are tailored to periodic domains, this architecture explicitly incorporates geometric information about the domain as well as Dirchlet or Neumann boundary conditions.

Since we are primarily interested in approximating the solution operator Γ+\Gamma^{+} for initial data u0∈𝒳u_{0}\in\mathcal{X}, we introduce a globally bounded and globally Lipschitz extension of the reaction term in the state variable.

Let U>0U>0 be chosen so that every mild solution corresponding to u0∈𝒳u_{0}\in\mathcal{X} satisfies

‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(Ω,ℝm)≤U,t∈[0,T0],\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{m})}\leq U,\qquad t\in[0,T_{0}],

where T0>0T_{0}>0 will be chosen below. Define the componentwise clipping map

𝒞U:ℝm→[−U,U]m\mathcal{C}_{U}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to[-U,U]^{m}

by

(𝒞U(z))j:=max{−U,min{zj,U}},j=1,…,m.(\mathcal{C}_{U}(z))_{j}:=\max\{-U,\min\{z_{j},U\}\},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.

We then define

(3.1) F~​(x,t,z):=F⁡(x,t,𝒞U​(z)).\widetilde{F}(x,t,z):=F(x,t,\mathcal{C}_{U}(z)).

Since 𝒞U\mathcal{C}_{U} is 11-Lipschitz, any Lipschitz bound for FF on

Ω¯×[0,T0]×[−U,U]m\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{0}]\times[-U,U]^{m}

extends to F~\widetilde{F} on Ω¯×[0,T0]×ℝm\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{0}]\times\mathbb{R}^{m} with the same constant. Moreover, F~\widetilde{F} is uniformly bounded in the state variable. Finally,

F~​(x,t,z)=F⁡(x,t,z)for ​z∈[−U,U]m,\widetilde{F}(x,t,z)=F(x,t,z)\qquad\text{for }z\in[-U,U]^{m},

so replacing FF by F~\widetilde{F} does not change any of the mild solutions under consideration.

We now state the main result.

Theorem 4.

Let n≥1n\geq 1, and let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a bounded domain with C2+αC^{2+\alpha} boundary. Let T~>0\tilde{T}>0. Assume that the clipped extension F~\widetilde{F} defined in (3.1) satisfies

(3.2) |F~​(x,t,u)|≤MF|\widetilde{F}(x,t,u)|\leq M_{F}

and

(3.3) |F~​(x,t,u)−F~​(y,s,v)|≤LF​(|x−y|+|t−s|+|u−v|)|\widetilde{F}(x,t,u)-\widetilde{F}(y,s,v)|\leq L_{F}\bigl(|x-y|+|t-s|+|u-v|\bigr)

for all

(x,t),(y,s)∈Ω¯×[0,T~],u,v∈ℝm,(x,t),(y,s)\in\bar{\Omega}\times[0,\tilde{T}],\qquad u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{m},

where MF,LF>0M_{F},L_{F}>0 are independent of uu and vv. Then there exists T0∈(0,T~]T_{0}\in(0,\tilde{T}] such that, for any ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), there exists a neural operator

Γ∈𝒩​𝒪ReLUL,H,N\Gamma\in\mathcal{NO}^{L,H,N}_{\mathrm{ReLU}}

satisfying

supu0∈𝒳‖Γ⁡(u0)−Γ+​(u0)‖L2​(0,T0,L2​(Ω,ℝm))≤ϵ.\sup_{u_{0}\in\mathcal{X}}\|\Gamma(u_{0})-\Gamma^{+}(u_{0})\|_{L^{2}(0,T_{0};L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{m}))}\leq\epsilon.

Moreover,

L⁡(Γ)≤C​(log⁡ϵ−1)2,H⁡(Γ)≤C​ϵ−(n+m+1)​(log⁡ϵ−1)2,L(\Gamma)\leq C(\log\epsilon^{-1})^{2},\qquad H(\Gamma)\leq C\epsilon^{-(n+m+1)}(\log\epsilon^{-1})^{2},

and

N⁡(Γ)≤C​ϵ−n,N(\Gamma)\leq C\epsilon^{-n},

where C>0C>0 is independent of ϵ\epsilon.

Theorem 4 shows that the depth grows at most squared logarithmically, and the total number of neurons and the spectral rank grows at most polynomially as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0. We emphasize that the Laplacian eigenfunction-based neural operator avoids the curse of parametric complexity, namely the exponential growth of parameters observed for general operator learning [22]. This theoretical finding is further supported by numerical experiments, where we compare the Laplacian eigenfunction-based neural operator with standard FNOs.

Lemma 5.

For this purpose, we use the standard positive-negative channel representation. For every scalar or vector quantity zz, define

The signed-channel representation increases the width by at most a constant factor and adds only a constant number of layers to each Picard block. 5. Numerical example

Motivated by the Laplacian spectral representation underlying the architecture analyzed above, we numerically investigate a Laplacian-eigenfunction-based spectral neural operator for a generalized Gierer-Meinhardt system and a Gray-Scott system. The numerical architecture is not intended to reproduce the time-integrated Picard architecture used in the proof of the main approximation theorem exactly. Instead, it evaluates the central architectural principle suggested by the theory: replacing a generic Fourier representation by the spectral basis of the Laplacian associated with the geometry and boundary conditions of the underlying PDE.We conduct three experiments: a Gierer-Meinhardt system on a square (Experiment I), a Gierer-Meinhardt system on a disk (Experiment II), and a Gray-Scott system on a square (Experiment III).

Following [18], we learn a one-step map from the current state to the next sampled state. For computational efficiency, we use this autoregressive formulation in place of the full-trajectory operator considered in the main approximation theorem. Let

0=t0<t1<⋯<tK=T0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{K}=T

denote the sampling times, and write zk=(utk,vtk)z_{k}=(u_{t_{k}},v_{t_{k}}) for the two-component state, using (U,V)(U,V) in Experiment III. For each fixed set of PDE parameters, we train a separate model Γ\Gamma to approximate

Γ(zk)≈zk+1,k=0,1,…,K−1.\Gamma(z_{k})\approx z_{k+1},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,K-1.

The training loss is the relative L2L^{2} error:

(5.1) ℒ=∑k=0K−1‖Γ⁡(zk)−zk+1‖L2​(Ω)2‖zk+1‖L2​(Ω)2.\mathcal{L}=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\frac{\|\Gamma(z_{k})-z_{k+1}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}}}{\|z_{k+1}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)^{2}}}.
z^k+1=Γ(z^k),k=0,1,…,K−1.\hat{z}_{k+1}=\Gamma(\hat{z}_{k}),\qquad k=0,1,\dots,K-1.

We compare the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), which uses Fourier modes for its spectral convolutions, with the Laplacian Eigenfunction Neural Operator (LENO), which uses a spectral basis associated with the Laplacian and the prescribed boundary conditions. On the square and the disk domains, we use the analytical Laplacian eigenfunctions for homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. In the FNO implementation on these domains, the input fields are padded before applying the Fourier transform.

Let p=1,…,100p=1,\dots,100 index trajectories and let {(xj,yj)}j=0Nspace−1\{(x_{j},y_{j})\}_{j=0}^{N_{\mathrm{space}}-1} denote the spatial sampling points. Each transition consists of a four-channel input and a two-channel target:

(5.2) Xk,j(p)\displaystyle X_{k,j}^{(p)} =(u(p)​(xj,yj,tk),v(p)​(xj,yj,tk),xj,yj),\displaystyle=\bigl(u^{(p)}(x_{j},y_{j},t_{k}),v^{(p)}(x_{j},y_{j},t_{k}),x_{j},y_{j}\bigr),
Yk,j(p)\displaystyle Y_{k,j}^{(p)} =(u(p)​(xj,yj,tk+1),v(p)​(xj,yj,tk+1)).\displaystyle=\bigl(u^{(p)}(x_{j},y_{j},t_{k+1}),v^{(p)}(x_{j},y_{j},t_{k+1})\bigr).

Here (u,v)(u,v) is replaced by (U,V)(U,V) in Experiment III, and NspaceN_{\mathrm{space}} counts spatial points. The scalar time increment is normalized by the final time of the corresponding experiment:

(5.3) δk=tk+1−tkT,Γ⁡(Xk(p),δk)≈Yk(p).\delta_{k}=\frac{t_{k+1}-t_{k}}{T},\qquad\Gamma\bigl(X_{k}^{(p)},\delta_{k}\bigr)\approx Y_{k}^{(p)}.

Thus, the model receives Xk(p)∈ℝNspace×4X_{k}^{(p)}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N_{\mathrm{space}}\times 4} and the separate scalar δk\delta_{k}, and returns the next state at the same points in ℝNspace×2{\mathbb{R}}^{N_{\mathrm{space}}\times 2}. During rollout, the predicted fields replace the field channels of the next input, while the coordinates remain fixed and the prescribed time increment is used.

The code used for the numerical experiments is available at https://github.com/zawa0073/LENO_public.

5.1. Experiment I: Gierer-Meinhardt system on a square

We consider the following parabolic system:

ut=0.1​Δ​u+0.5​(u2(1+p​u2)​v−u),in ​Ω×(0,T),\displaystyle u_{t}=0.1\Delta u+0.5\Bigl(\dfrac{u^{2}}{(1+pu^{2})\,v}-u\Bigr),\quad\text{in }\Omega\times(0,T),
vt=2.0​Δ​v+0.5​(u2−0.9​v),in ​Ω×[0,T],\displaystyle v_{t}=2.0\Delta v+0.5\bigl(u^{2}-0.9\,v\bigr),\quad\text{in }\Omega\times[0,T],
∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,on ​∂Ω×[0,T],\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega\times[0,T],
u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),in Ω¯,\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),\quad\text{in }\overline{\Omega},
∂u0∂ν=∂v0∂ν=0,on ​∂Ω.\displaystyle\frac{\partial u_{0}}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v_{0}}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega.

where

x∈Ω=[0,200]×[0,200],t∈[0,250].x\in\Omega=[0,200]\times[0,200],\qquad t\in[0,250].

We generate random initial conditions by perturbing a steady equilibrium (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) as

(5.5) u0=u∗+0.05​ξu,v0=v∗+0.05​ξv,u_{0}=u^{*}+0.05\,\xi_{u},\qquad v_{0}=v^{*}+0.05\,\xi_{v},

where ξu\xi_{u} and ξv\xi_{v} are sampled independently from a standard normal distribution on the spatial grid (i.i.d. across grid points). Thus, the perturbations are additive Gaussian noise with an absolute standard deviation of 0.050.05 in each component. We parametrize the equilibrium by a scalar s>0s>0:

u∗=s,v∗=s20.9.u^{*}=s,\qquad v^{*}=\frac{s^{2}}{0.9}.

Based on [32], the parameter pp is chosen so that

11+p​s2=s0.9.\frac{1}{1+ps^{2}}=\frac{s}{0.9}.

We consider the two parameter values

s∈{0.785, 0.85}.s\in\{0.785,\ 0.85\}.

For each value of ss, the dataset consists of 9090 training trajectories and 1010 test trajectories, each pairing a random initial condition with its numerical solution.

We discretize the spatial domain Ω\Omega using a uniform 200×200200\times 200 grid. In time, we employ a non-uniform discretization that is denser near the initial transient, where the dynamics change most rapidly, and coarser afterward. Specifically, we use the time grid t∈{0,1,2,…,50,100,150,200,250}t\in\{0,1,2,\dots,50,100,150,200,250\} , and store the input coordinates in normalized form:

(5.6) (x,y)↦(x200,y200)∈[0,1]2,t↦t250.(x,y)\mapsto\Bigl(\frac{x}{200},\frac{y}{200}\Bigr)\in[0,1]^{2},\qquad t\mapsto\frac{t}{250}.

Both models have depth 44 and channel width 6464. LENO uses 96×9696\times 96 spectral modes, whereas FNO uses 48×4848\times 48 Fourier modes. The LENO truncation is chosen with reference to the Nyquist–Shannon sampling criterion, balancing predictive accuracy and computational cost. The two networks have approximately 151×106151\times 10^{6} trainable parameters. We use Adam with an initial learning rate of 10−310^{-3}, halve the learning rate every 5050 epochs, and train for 200200 epochs with a batch size of 88. These optimization settings are identical for FNO and LENO.

5.2. Experiment II: Gierer-Meinhardt system on a disk

In the second experiment, we compare FNO and LENO on a domain with a curved boundary. Following the saturated Gierer-Meinhardt model studied by Moyles and Ward [28], we consider

(5.7) ut\displaystyle u_{t} =d1​Δ​u−u+u2v⁡(1+σ​u2),\displaystyle=d_{1}\Delta u-u+\frac{u^{2}}{v(1+\sigma u^{2})}, in ​Ω×(0,T),\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega\times(0,T),
vt\displaystyle v_{t} =d2​Δ​v−v+u2d1,\displaystyle=d_{2}\Delta v-v+\frac{u^{2}}{\sqrt{d_{1}}}, in ​Ω×(0,T),\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega\times(0,T),
∂u∂ν\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu} =∂v∂ν=0,\displaystyle=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0, on ​∂Ω×[0,T],\displaystyle\text{on }\partial\Omega\times[0,T],
u⁡(x,y,0)\displaystyle u(x,y,0) =u0(x,y),v(x,y,0)=v0(x,y),\displaystyle=u_{0}(x,y),\qquad v(x,y,0)=v_{0}(x,y), in ​Ω¯,\displaystyle\text{in }\overline{\Omega},

where the spatial domain is the unit disk and the final time is T=50T=50:

Ω={(x,y)∈ℝ2:x2+y2<1},t∈[0,50].\Omega=\{(x,y)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}:x^{2}+y^{2}<1\},\qquad t\in[0,50].

Here, d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} are the diffusion coefficients, and σ\sigma controls the saturation of the activator production term. In terms of the radial coordinate r=x2+y2r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}, the boundary conditions are ur=vr=0u_{r}=v_{r}=0 at r=1r=1. Here, ur=∂u/∂ru_{r}=\partial u/\partial r and vr=∂v/∂rv_{r}=\partial v/\partial r. On the circular boundary, the outward unit normal is the radial unit vector, so these derivatives coincide with the outward normal derivatives, without assuming radial symmetry. Moyles and Ward [28, Section 5, p. 629] describe vanishing radial derivatives at the origin as a compatibility condition in their numerical scheme. In our cell-centered discretization, the origin is not a grid point; its treatment is specified by the radial flux discretization below. Vanishing radial derivatives at the origin follow from smoothness for radially symmetric fields, but are not a general regularity requirement for fields with angular dependence.

We generate the initial conditions by perturbing a spatially homogeneous positive equilibrium (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}):

(5.8) u0=u∗+5×10−4​ξu,v0=v∗+5×10−4​ξv,u_{0}=u^{*}+5\times 10^{-4}\,\xi_{u},\qquad v_{0}=v^{*}+5\times 10^{-4}\,\xi_{v},

where ξu\xi_{u} and ξv\xi_{v} are sampled independently from the uniform distribution 𝒰⁡(−1,1)\mathcal{U}(-1,1) at each spatial grid point. The noise therefore has zero mean and an absolute amplitude of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} in each component. The equilibrium can be parametrized as

We consider two parameter configurations:

(5.10) (d1,d2,σ)∈{(0.025,1,25),(0.01,0.01,5910)}.(\sqrt{d_{1}},d_{2},\sigma)\in\{(0.025,1,25),\ (0.01,0.01,5910)\}.

The corresponding equilibrium values are listed in Table 1. For each configuration, FNO and LENO are trained separately using the one-step prediction formulation, and their predictions are advanced by autoregressive rollout. This experiment extends the comparison in Experiment I to a nonrectangular domain with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.

For each parameter configuration, the teacher dataset contains 100100 trajectories sampled at

(5.11) tk=k,k=0,1,…,50.t_{k}=k,\qquad k=0,1,\dots,50.

Each trajectory therefore provides 5151 saved states and 5050 consecutive one-step transitions, with normalized increment δk=1/50=0.02\delta_{k}=1/50=0.02.

We sample the disk on a polar grid with Nr=128N_{r}=128 radial points and Nθ=256N_{\theta}=256 angular points:

(5.12) ri\displaystyle r_{i} =i+1/2Nr,\displaystyle=\frac{i+1/2}{N_{r}}, i=0,…,Nr−1,\displaystyle i=0,\dots,N_{r}-1,
θj\displaystyle\theta_{j} =2​π​jNθ,\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi j}{N_{\theta}}, j=0,…,Nθ−1,\displaystyle j=0,\dots,N_{\theta}-1,
(xi​j,yi​j)\displaystyle(x_{ij},y_{ij}) =(ricosθj,risinθj).\displaystyle=(r_{i}\cos\theta_{j},r_{i}\sin\theta_{j}).

This gives Nspace=128×256=32768N_{\mathrm{space}}=128\times 256=32768 sampling points. The radial coordinates are cell centers, so neither r=0r=0 nor r=1r=1 is included as a sampling point. The teacher solver discretizes the radial Laplacian in flux form. It sets the outer radial flux to zero and uses a zero inner-face flux contribution at the origin, where the radial face weight vanishes. This inner-face treatment does not independently enforce pointwise values of uru_{r} and vrv_{r} at r=0r=0. The angular discretization is periodic. At each pair of consecutive saved states, the fields and Cartesian coordinates form the input in (5.2), together with δk\delta_{k}.

For LENO, we use the Neumann eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on the disk. For a disk of radius RR, the eigenvalue problem is

(5.13) −Δ​ϕn,m=λn,m​ϕn,min ​Ω,∂ϕn,m∂r=0at ​r=R.-\Delta\phi_{n,m}=\lambda_{n,m}\phi_{n,m}\quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad\frac{\partial\phi_{n,m}}{\partial r}=0\quad\text{at }r=R.

Let JnJ_{n} denote the Bessel function of the first kind of order nn, and let αn,m\alpha_{n,m} be its mmth positive derivative zero:

(5.14) Jn′​(αn,m)=0,λn,m=(αn,mR)2.J_{n}^{\prime}(\alpha_{n,m})=0,\qquad\lambda_{n,m}=\left(\frac{\alpha_{n,m}}{R}\right)^{2}.

(5.15) ϕn,mc​(r,θ)\displaystyle\phi_{n,m}^{\mathrm{c}}(r,\theta) =Jn​(αn,m​rR)​cos⁡(n​θ),\displaystyle=J_{n}\!\left(\frac{\alpha_{n,m}r}{R}\right)\cos(n\theta), n≥0,m≥1,\displaystyle n\geq 0,\ m\geq 1,
ϕn,ms​(r,θ)\displaystyle\phi_{n,m}^{\mathrm{s}}(r,\theta) =Jn​(αn,m​rR)​sin⁡(n​θ),\displaystyle=J_{n}\!\left(\frac{\alpha_{n,m}r}{R}\right)\sin(n\theta), n≥1,m≥1.\displaystyle n\geq 1,\ m\geq 1.

The constant eigenfunction with eigenvalue zero is also included. In this experiment, R=1R=1, and the basis is truncated in ascending order of the eigenvalues.

For FNO, we place the disk inside a surrounding Cartesian square and set the field values outside the disk to zero before applying the FFT. The spectral convolutions use Fourier modes exp⁡(i⁡(kx​x+ky​y))\exp\!\bigl(\mathrm{i}(k_{x}x+k_{y}y)\bigr) on this square. Thus, LENO represents the fields in a basis defined on the disk with Neumann boundary conditions, while FNO applies Fourier convolutions to the fields extended by zero to the square.

Both models have depth 44 and channel width 6464. LENO uses 20482048 spectral modes, whereas FNO uses 23×2323\times 23 Fourier modes. The LENO truncation is selected using the reconstruction error obtained by projecting the teacher fields onto the retained basis functions, balancing predictive accuracy and computational cost. The two networks have approximately 33×10633\times 10^{6} trainable parameters. We use Adam with an initial learning rate of 10−310^{-3}, halve the learning rate every 5050 epochs, and train for 200200 epochs with a batch size of 3232. These optimization settings are identical for FNO and LENO.

5.4. Numerical results

In all six tested configurations, LENO achieved lower relative L2L^{2} errors on the test trajectories than FNO. The difference was small in Experiment I, whereas it was particularly pronounced in Experiment II on the disk. In Experiment III, LENO also yielded substantially smaller values of the measured normal derivative ∇u⋅n\nabla u\cdot n, while the improvement in relative L2L^{2} error depended on the parameter configuration. LENO achieved lower mean relative L2L^{2} rollout errors than FNO in both configurations of Experiments I and II, with the largest reduction occurring in Experiment II at σ=25\sigma=25. In Experiment III, FNO achieved lower mean relative L2L^{2} rollout errors in both configurations: 35.87%35.87\% versus 36.72%36.72\% for F=0.0125F=0.0125, and 27.58%27.58\% versus 35.64%35.64\% for F=0.024F=0.024, where each pair lists FNO followed by LENO. Nevertheless, LENO yielded smaller ∇u^⋅n\nabla\hat{u}\cdot n, in all six configurations. Thus, in Experiment III, the smaller boundary residuals did not translate into smaller relative L2L^{2} rollout errors. In all comparisons, FNO and LENO used the same initial values for their network parameters. The same random seed was used to initialize FNO and LENO, with architecture-specific initialization of their spectral layers.

The pronounced improvement on the disk may partly be due to the choice of spectral basis. On the square, the Neumann Laplacian eigenfunctions are products of trigonometric functions and are relatively close in form to Fourier functions. On the disk, they have Bessel-function radial components and trigonometric angular components, reflecting the geometry and boundary conditions more directly. This difference in spectral basis may contribute to LENO’s stronger performance in Experiment II.

In Experiment III, the difference in relative L2L^{2} error arose mainly at early times. During this phase, the patterns propagated outward from the center within the interior, while the fields near the boundary remained in the uniform trivial state (U,V)=(1,0)(U,V)=(1,0). Since the fields were constant near all four sides, their periodic extensions were continuous and their normal derivatives were zero. Thus, the periodicity assumption of FNO was not violated during this phase, leaving no opportunity for LENO’s advantage in handling the boundary conditions to manifest itself. At later times, the predictions of both models became uncorrelated with the teacher solution, and the relative L2L^{2} error no longer distinguished their performance. Consequently, the overall relative L2L^{2} error was determined by the ability to track the early-phase dynamics. In this experiment, LENO lost track of these dynamics earlier, resulting in a smaller error for FNO.

Training and test losses (Figures 1-6).

The blue and orange curves represent the FNO training and test losses, respectively; the gray and yellow curves represent the LENO training and test losses, respectively. Both training and test losses are recorded at every epoch. The loss measures the discrepancy between the one-step operator prediction and the corresponding reference data.

Color maps of predicted solutions (Figures 7-12).

The color maps show the full solution fields obtained by repeatedly applying the trained one-step operator, starting from the initial conditions in the test dataset.

Time evolution of the L2L^{2} error (Figures 13-18).

These plots show the L2L^{2} error over the entire spatial domain as a function of time. The predicted solutions are obtained by repeatedly applying the trained one-step operator, starting from the initial conditions in the test dataset.

The L2L^{2} errors in the benchmark tables are evaluated over the full solution trajectories obtained by repeatedly applying the trained one-step operator. The normal derivative ∇u^⋅n\nabla\hat{u}\cdot n is evaluated on the same predicted trajectories, where nn denotes the outward unit normal and u^\hat{u} denotes the predicted first component (U^\hat{U} in Experiment III). All entries are reported as the mean and standard deviation over NN test trajectories.

Reconstruction errors.

Tables 8-13 report the mean and maximum relative L2L^{2} reconstruction errors for the input and target fields in the training data. The reconstruction settings and displayed precision follow the source tables.

6. Conclusion

In this work, we established a quantitative approximation theory for Laplacian-based neural operators applied to nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. By exploiting the spectral representation of the diffusion semigroup and the mild formulation of the PDE, we constructed a neural operator that approximates the associated Picard iteration and obtained explicit bounds on its approximation error and spectral rank. Our numerical experiments further showed that using Laplacian eigenfunctions can improve prediction accuracy over a Fourier-based model, with the most pronounced improvement observed on the disk domain.

The analysis suggests that eigenfunction expansions provide a natural framework for incorporating PDE geometry and boundary conditions into neural operator approximation theory. An important direction for future work is to extend this spectral approach to other classes of PDEs and to identify the corresponding quantitative approximation bounds. Our experiments used an autoregressive one-step model for computational efficiency, rather than the time-integrated Picard architecture constructed in the proof. Implementing and evaluating that architecture would help determine whether its theoretical guarantees can be realized in a practical model.
